title: Application-Level Caching
description: Understand in-memory and distributed caches used inside applications to reduce latency and database load.

data.text: Application-level caching stores frequently accessed data in memory or a dedicated caching layer between the application and the database. By keeping hot data close to the application code, you avoid repeated expensive database queries and dramatically improve read performance. This layer is especially valuable for data that changes infrequently but is read very often.

data.title: Frequently Used Patterns:
items: Cache-aside: The application reads from the cache first and falls back to the database on a miss.
Write-through: Writes go to both the cache and the database simultaneously, keeping them synchronized.
Write-behind: Writes update the cache first and are flushed to the database asynchronously for higher write throughput.
Read-through: The cache itself loads missing data from the database transparently.

data.text: The two most common application caches are Redis and Memcached. Redis supports rich data structures, persistence, replication, and pub/sub, making it a better fit when you need more than simple key-value storage. Memcached is simpler and excels at pure object caching with very high throughput and low memory overhead. Choose Redis when you need data structures, expiration policies, or persistence. Choose Memcached when you need a lightweight, multi-node, volatile cache for session data or query results.

data.title: Common Pitfall
data.text: Caching adds complexity. Without proper invalidation, size limits, and fallback logic, a cache can return stale data, exhaust memory, or become a single point of failure.

rows: Strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets

data.text: Application caches live in memory, so capacity is finite. You must configure a maximum memory limit and choose an eviction policy such as LRU, LFU, or TTL-based expiration. LRU removes the least recently used items, which works well for temporal locality. LFU removes the least frequently used items, which is better when access patterns skew toward a stable hot set. Monitoring hit ratio, eviction count, and memory usage helps you tune the cache size and TTLs before production incidents occur.

data.title: Design Exercise: Session Cache
data.description: You are adding a session cache to a web app with 2 million daily active users and 30-minute session TTLs.
steps: Estimate the number of concurrent sessions assuming a 1:7 peak-to-daily ratio.
Choose between Redis and Memcached and justify your choice.
Propose an eviction policy and TTL strategy.
Identify one failure mode if the cache becomes unavailable.
data.expectedOutcome: A concise cache design document that addresses capacity, tooling, and resilience.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Application caches reduce database load and read latency
Redis and Memcached serve different use cases
Eviction policies and TTLs control memory usage
Monitor hit ratio and eviction metrics in production
data.takeaway: Effective application caching starts with the right data access pattern, then selects the tool and eviction strategy that matches your workload.
